title: Bash Quoting & Expansion: Field Notes
summary: A dense field guide to how Bash turns a line of text into an argument vector — quoting rules, the ordered expansion pipeline, word splitting, globbing, parameter expansion operators, and arrays. Ends with the rules that make quoting-everything the default and the gotchas that punish anyone who forgets.

chapters.title: The Shell Reads a Line: Order of Operations
points: Bash processes a command in a fixed order: tokenize/quote removal is interleaved with brace expansion, tilde expansion, parameter/variable expansion, command substitution, arithmetic expansion, word splitting, filename expansion (globbing), then quote removal, then redirection setup, then execve.
Critical fact: word splitting and globbing happen AFTER variable expansion — the shell never re-parses your variable's contents for quotes or operators, but it does split and glob them.
This is why `$x` where x='a b' yields two arguments, but where x='a;b' yields ONE argument `a;b` — the `;` is not re-interpreted as a command separator.
Brace expansion is FIRST and is purely textual: `{a,b}c` -> `ac bc`; it never looks at the filesystem, so `{1..3}.txt` produces names whether files exist or not.
Brace expansion happens before parameter expansion, so `{1..$n}` does NOT work — the range is fixed before `$n` is known. Use `seq` or a C-style for loop.
Tilde expansion: `~` -> $HOME, `~user` -> that user's home, `~+` -> $PWD, `~-` -> $OLDPWD. Only unquoted, only at the start of a word or after `:` in assignments.
Quote removal is the LAST step: the quotes themselves are never passed to the command. `echo "hi"` sends the 2 bytes `hi` to echo.
Command substitution `$(cmd)` runs cmd in a subshell, captures stdout, and strips ALL trailing newlines — not just one.
Arithmetic expansion `$(( ))` evaluates integer math; inside it, bare names are auto-dereferenced, so `$((x+1))` and `$((\$x+1))` both work.
Process substitution `<(cmd)` expands to a filename like `/dev/fd/63` — it is a path, not text, and works where a file argument is needed: `diff <(sort a) <(sort b)`.
Redirections are set up after expansions but are parsed as syntax up front: `> $file` splits the filename if unquoted, and Bash errors with 'ambiguous redirect'.
Assignments are a special context: `x=$y` needs no quotes because word splitting and globbing are suppressed on the right-hand side of a plain assignment.
Mental model to memorize: 'the shell expands, then splits, then globs, then strips quotes' — every gotchas in this handbook falls out of that one sentence.
Debug the pipeline with `set -x` or, better, a printf argument dumper: `printf '[%s]\n' $var` shows exactly how many arguments were produced.

chapters.title: The Three Quotes: Single, Double, Backslash
points: Single quotes `'...'` are literal and total: nothing expands, no escapes work, and you cannot put a single quote inside them by any means.
To include a single quote, end the quoting and re-open: `'it'\''s'` — four pieces concatenated into one word `it's`.
Double quotes `"..."` allow `$`, backtick, `\`, and `!` (with history expansion in interactive shells); everything else is literal.
Inside double quotes, backslash only escapes `$`, backtick, `"`, `\`, and newline. `"\n"` is a literal backslash-n, not a newline.
Backslash outside quotes escapes any single next character: `a\ b` is one word `a b`.
Adjacent quoted and unquoted pieces concatenate with no separator: `"$HOME"/bin/'my app'` is one word.
`$'...'` is ANSI-C quoting: interprets `\n`, `\t`, `\x41`, `\u00e9`. Use `$'\t'` to get a real tab into IFS or a delimiter.
`$"..."` is locale translation quoting — rare, and it silently behaves like `"..."` when no translation catalog exists.
Globs are literal inside ANY quoting: `"*.txt"` matches a file actually named `*.txt`, not all text files.
Quoting does not nest: inside `'...'` a `"` is just a character; inside `"..."` a `'` is just a character.
Comparison row — expands variables: double YES, single NO, backslash NO. Blocks splitting: double YES, single YES, backslash YES (per char).
Comparison row — allows literal `$`: single YES, double only via `\$`, backslash YES.
Rule of thumb: use double quotes when you want expansion, single quotes for fixed literal text (regexes, awk programs, sed scripts), backslash for a single stray metacharacter.
`"$@"` is a documented special case, not a normal double-quoted string — covered in the arrays chapter.

chapters.title: Word Splitting and IFS
points: Word splitting applies ONLY to the results of unquoted parameter expansion, command substitution, and arithmetic expansion — never to literal text you typed.
`echo a   b` prints `a b` because the parser collapses the literal whitespace as token separators, which is a different mechanism from word splitting.
IFS (Internal Field Separator) controls splitting; the default is space, tab, newline.
Whitespace IFS characters are special: runs of them are collapsed and leading/trailing ones are ignored. `x='  a   b  '; f $x` gives 2 fields.
Non-whitespace IFS characters are NOT collapsed: with `IFS=:`, the value `a::b` splits into 3 fields, one of them empty — this is exactly how $PATH's empty entry means '.'.
Setting `IFS=` (empty) disables word splitting entirely for that scope.
Idiom: `IFS=: read -r a b c <<< "$line"` — the IFS prefix applies only to that `read` command, no cleanup needed.
`read -r` is mandatory: without `-r`, `read` treats backslash as a line-continuation and escape character, mangling data.
`while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file` is the only correct line-reading loop: `IFS=` preserves leading/trailing whitespace, `-r` preserves backslashes.
`for x in $(cat file)` is a classic bug: it splits on all whitespace, so filenames with spaces shatter, and glob characters in the file expand.
Deliberate splitting is legitimate — `arr=($string)` with a chosen IFS is the standard split-a-string-into-array idiom; it is unquoted ON PURPOSE.
Splitting happens before globbing, so each resulting field is then independently glob-matched — a field of `*` becomes many arguments.
`set -f` (noglob) disables globbing so you can split without glob damage; `set +f` restores it.
Null fields: unquoted `$x` where x is empty produces ZERO arguments, not one empty argument. `"$x"` produces exactly one empty argument.

chapters.title: Globbing / Pathname Expansion
points: Glob operators: `*` matches any string including empty (but never `/`), `?` matches exactly one character, `[abc]`/`[a-z]`/`[!0-9]` match a character class.
Globs are NOT regexes: `*` in a glob means 'any characters', in a regex it means 'zero or more of the previous atom'.
POSIX classes inside brackets: `[[:digit:]]`, `[[:alpha:]]`, `[[:space:]]` — locale-aware and safer than `[a-z]` ranges.
Leading dots are not matched by `*` — hidden files require an explicit `.*` or `shopt -s dotglob`.
`shopt -s nullglob` makes a non-matching glob expand to nothing instead of to itself. Without it, `for f in *.txt` runs once with the literal string `*.txt` when there are no matches.
`shopt -s failglob` makes a non-matching glob an error — good for scripts that must not proceed silently.
`shopt -s globstar` enables `**` for recursive descent: `**/*.log`. Note `**` follows symlinked directories in older Bash.
`shopt -s extglob` adds `?(p)`, `*(p)`, `+(p)`, `@(p)`, `!(p)` — e.g. `rm !(keep.txt)` removes everything except keep.txt.
`shopt -s nocaseglob` makes matching case-insensitive.
Globbing is done by the SHELL, not the program: `ls *.txt` hands ls a list of names; ls never sees the asterisk.
Consequence: a glob matching 100k files can exceed ARG_MAX and fail with 'Argument list too long' — use `find -exec ... +` or `xargs` instead.
A glob result is never word-split further and needs no quotes: filenames with spaces survive `for f in *` intact.
Quoting a glob disables it: `"*.txt"` and `'*.txt'` are literal. This is why `find . -name '*.txt'` quotes the pattern — find, not the shell, must do the matching.
Filenames starting with `-` become options: use `./*` or `-- ` to guard, e.g. `rm -- *`.
`[[ $f == *.txt ]]` does glob matching inside a test; the right-hand side must be UNQUOTED to act as a pattern.

chapters.title: Parameter Expansion I: Defaults and Testing
points: `${var}` braces are needed to disambiguate: `${var}name` vs `$varname`.
`${var:-default}` — use default if var is unset OR empty; does not assign.
`${var-default}` — colon omitted means only UNSET triggers the default; an empty var stays empty. The colon is the unset-vs-empty switch across all these operators.
`${var:=default}` — use default AND assign it back to var. Cannot be used on positional parameters.
`${var:?message}` — expand var, or print message to stderr and exit a non-interactive shell. The one-line way to enforce required inputs.
`${var:+alt}` — expand alt only if var is set and non-empty; expands to nothing otherwise. Ideal for conditional flags: `cmd ${verbose:+--verbose}`.
`${#var}` gives the character length of the value; `${#arr[@]}` gives the element count of an array.
`${!var}` is indirect expansion: if var='HOME', `${!var}` yields the value of $HOME.
`${!prefix*}` and `${!prefix@}` list all variable names starting with prefix — useful for enumerating config vars.
Positional parameters: `$1..$9`, and `${10}` upward requires braces.
`$#` argument count, `$?` last exit status, `$$` PID, `$!` last background PID, `$0` script name, `$-` current option flags.
Comparison table to memorize — var unset / var='' / var='x' against `${var:-d}` gives d / d / x, and `${var-d}` gives d / '' / x.
All these operators still need quotes around the whole expansion: `"${var:-default}"`, because the default text is itself subject to word splitting.
Gotcha: `${var:?}` with an empty message still errors with a default message, which is a fine terse guard.

chapters.title: Parameter Expansion II: Slicing, Trimming, Substitution
points: `${var#pattern}` removes the shortest matching PREFIX; `${var##pattern}` removes the longest.
`${var%pattern}` removes the shortest matching SUFFIX; `${var%%pattern}` removes the longest.
Memory hook: on a US keyboard `#` is left of `%`, and `#` trims from the left.
Pure-shell basename: `${path##*/}`. Pure-shell dirname: `${path%/*}`. Both are faster than forking basename/dirname and are safe with newlines in names.
Strip an extension: `${file%.*}`. Get the extension: `${file##*.}`.
The patterns are GLOBS, not regexes, and must be unquoted to act as patterns — quoting them makes them literal.
`${var/old/new}` replaces the first match; `${var//old/new}` replaces all matches.
`${var/#old/new}` anchors the replacement to the start; `${var/%old/new}` anchors it to the end.
Deleting is replacing with nothing: `${var//[[:space:]]/}` strips all whitespace.
`${var:offset}` and `${var:offset:length}` slice substrings, zero-indexed. Negative offsets need a space or parens: `${var: -3}` for the last three characters.
Case modification (Bash 4+): `${var^}` upper first char, `${var^^}` upper all, `${var,}` lower first, `${var,,}` lower all.
`${var@Q}` quotes the value so it can be safely re-parsed by the shell — the correct way to build a command string for `eval` or `ssh`.
Other `@` transforms: `${var@U}` uppercase, `${var@E}` interpret escapes, `${var@A}` emit a reusable assignment statement.
Applied to an array with `[@]`, most of these operators apply element-wise: `${arr[@]%.txt}` strips the extension from every element.
These operators cost no fork, so a loop of `${x##*/}` is dramatically faster than a loop calling `basename` — the difference is process-creation time, roughly milliseconds each, per iteration.

chapters.title: Arrays: Indexed and Associative
points: Declare and assign: `arr=(a b c)` or `declare -a arr`; elements are whitespace-separated words subject to the normal expansions.
Index from zero: `${arr[0]}`. Braces are mandatory — `$arr[0]` expands `$arr` then the literal `[0]`.
Bare `$arr` means `${arr[0]}`, not the whole array — a very common source of silent bugs.
`"${arr[@]}"` expands to one properly-quoted word PER ELEMENT. This is the correct form 95% of the time.
`"${arr[*]}"` joins all elements into ONE word, separated by the first character of IFS. Use it only when you deliberately want a single joined string.
Unquoted `${arr[@]}` re-splits and re-globs every element — it destroys elements containing spaces.
`${#arr[@]}` is the element count; `${#arr[0]}` is the length of element zero.
`${!arr[@]}` lists the INDICES, which matters because indexed arrays can be sparse after `unset arr[1]`.
Append with `arr+=(new)`; the parentheses are required — `arr+=new` appends to element zero.
Slice an array: `"${arr[@]:1:2}"`. Slice the positional parameters the same way: `"${@:2}"` for 'all arguments after the first'.
Associative arrays require `declare -A map` FIRST; without it, Bash treats the subscript as arithmetic and everything collapses into index 0.
Associative usage: `map[key]=value`, `"${map[key]}"`, keys via `"${!map[@]}"`, values via `"${map[@]}"`. Iteration order is unspecified (hash order), not insertion order.
Build an array safely from find: `mapfile -d '' files < <(find . -print0)` — handles every legal filename including newlines.
`mapfile -t lines < file` reads a file into an array, `-t` stripping trailing newlines.
The killer use case: arrays are the only correct way to build a command with variable arguments — `cmd=(rsync -a); [[ $dry ]] && cmd+=(--dry-run); "${cmd[@]}" src dst`. No eval, no quoting damage.

chapters.title: "$@" vs $*: Passing Arguments Through
points: `"$@"` expands to `"$1" "$2" ...` — each positional parameter as its own separate, fully-quoted word.
`"$*"` expands to `"$1c$2c..."` — one single word, joined by the first character of IFS (a space by default).
Unquoted `$@` and unquoted `$*` are IDENTICAL and both wrong: both split and glob every argument.
Special empty case: with zero arguments, `"$@"` expands to zero words, while `"$*"` expands to one empty word. This is why `"$@"` is safe in `cmd "$@"`.
Comparison row — args are `a` and `b c`: `"$@"` gives 2 arguments; `"$*"` gives 1 argument `a b c`; `$@` gives 3 arguments.
Forwarding wrapper, correct form: `exec real-command "$@"` — preserves argument boundaries exactly.
Function arguments shadow script arguments: inside a function `$1` is the function's first argument, but `$0` remains the script name.
`shift` drops `$1` and renumbers; `shift n` drops n. `shift` past the end returns non-zero, which makes `while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]` loops safe.
`set -- a b c` replaces the positional parameters — the standard trick for re-parsing arguments after getopts.
`"${@:2}"` is all arguments from the second on; `"${@:$#}"` is the last argument.
Legitimate uses of `"$*"`: joining for a log message, or with a custom IFS to build a delimited string — `(IFS=,; echo "$*")` prints a CSV row.
In `for x; do ...; done` the implicit list is `"$@"` — already correctly quoted, which is why the bare form is safe and idiomatic.
Never write `cmd $*` in a wrapper script; it is the single most common way scripts break on paths containing spaces.
`"$@"` inside an array assignment: `args=("$@")` copies the arguments preserving boundaries.

chapters.title: Gotchas: Where Missing Quotes Bite
points: `rm -rf $dir/` with an empty `$dir` becomes `rm -rf /`. With quotes it becomes `rm -rf "/"` only if dir is truly empty — so also guard with `${dir:?dir is required}`.
`[ $x = y ]` with an empty or multi-word `$x` becomes a syntax error ('unary operator expected'); `[ "$x" = y ]` is correct. Legacy workaround `[ "x$x" = xy ]` exists because of this.
Prefer `[[ ... ]]` in Bash: it is shell syntax, so no word splitting or globbing happens on its operands — but quoting is still required on the RIGHT side of `==` unless you want glob matching.
`echo $var` collapses whitespace and expands globs in the value; `printf '%s\n' "$var"` is the reliable output primitive.
`echo` is not portable for arbitrary data: it may interpret `-n`, `-e`, or backslashes depending on shell and options. Use `printf`.
Filenames with a leading dash are parsed as options — `rm -- "$f"` or `rm "./$f"`.
Filenames may legally contain spaces, newlines, quotes, and glob characters. The only two bytes forbidden are `/` and NUL — which is why `find -print0` / `xargs -0` / `mapfile -d ''` exist.
Command substitution strips trailing newlines, so `x=$(cat f)` loses them; work around with `x=$(cat f; printf x); x=${x%x}`.
`$(...)` nests cleanly and is the modern form; backticks require escaping backslashes on each nesting level and should be retired.
Unquoted expansion inside a redirection is an 'ambiguous redirect' error when it produces zero or multiple words: `> $f` fails where `> "$f"` works.
`eval` re-parses its argument through the entire expansion pipeline a second time — every character of user data becomes shell code. Avoid it; use arrays or `${var@Q}` if you truly must.
Building a remote command for `ssh host "$cmd"` re-parses on the remote side: quote with `${cmd@Q}` or use `printf %q`.
`export VAR=$(cmd)` masks the exit status of cmd — the assignment's status wins. Split the assignment from the export when checking failures.
`set -e` does not fire inside a command substitution used in an assignment, nor for any command whose status is tested — do not rely on it as a safety net.
Numeric contexts are the one place quotes are optional: inside `$(( ))` and array subscripts, splitting does not happen.

chapters.title: Rules, Tools, and the Checklist
points: Rule 1: quote every expansion by default — `"$var"`, `"$(cmd)"`, `"${arr[@]}"`. The exceptions are few and deliberate.
Rule 2: the deliberate exceptions are — inside `[[ ]]` and `(( ))`, the right side of a plain assignment `x=$y`, when you want splitting into an array, and when a glob pattern must stay a pattern.
Rule 3: use arrays, never a string, to hold a list of arguments or filenames.
Rule 4: use `"$@"` to forward arguments; use `"$*"` only to build one deliberate joined string.
Rule 5: use `-print0` / `-0` / `-d ''` whenever data crosses a process boundary as a list of filenames.
Rule 6: use `printf '%s\n'` instead of `echo` for data you do not control.
Rule 7: use parameter expansion (`${p##*/}`, `${f%.*}`) instead of forking basename/dirname/sed for simple string surgery.
Script preamble worth memorizing: `set -euo pipefail` plus `IFS=$'\n\t'` — knowing `set -e` has the holes listed in the gotchas chapter.
`shellcheck` catches the majority of quoting bugs statically; SC2086 ('Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting') is the single most common finding in the wild.
Debug harness: `printf '<%s>\n' "$@"` inside a function shows exactly how many arguments arrived and where their boundaries are.
`set -x` prints commands after expansion; Bash 4.4+ quotes the trace output so argument boundaries are visible.
`declare -p var` prints a variable with its type and full quoting — the fastest way to see whether something is a string, an indexed array, or associative.
Portability note: arrays, `${var,,}`, `${var@Q}`, `mapfile`, and `[[ ]]` are Bash features, absent from POSIX `sh` — a `#!/bin/sh` script must fall back to `"$@"`, `case`, and `set --`.

Closing summary: the shell expands, then splits, then globs, then strips quotes; quotes are what turn off the splitting and globbing steps; arrays are what preserve boundaries that a single string cannot.

One-line takeaway to leave on the last page: if a variable is not inside double quotes, you have promised the shell it contains no spaces, no globs, and no surprises — and filenames break that promise every day.
